div.p: Scheduling is a central yet challenging problem in real-time embedded systems. The Clock Constraint Specification Language (CCSL) provides a formalism to specify logical constraints of events in real-time embedded systems. A prerequisite for the events is that they must be schedulable under constraints. That is, there must be a schedule which controls all events to occur infinitely often. Schedulability analysis of CCSL raises important algorithmic problems such as computational complexity and design of efficient decision procedures. In this work, we compare the scheduling problems of CCSL specifications to the real-time scheduling problem. We show how to encode a simple task model in CCSL and discuss some benefits and differences compared to more classical scheduling strategies.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Classical Real-Time Schedulability [1] usually relies on task models, arrival patterns and constraints (e.g., precedence, resources) to propose algorithms for the schedulability problem with analytical results [2] or heuristics depending on the specific model (e.g., priorities, preemptive). There are other solutions based on timed automata [3], [4], [5], timed petri nets [6], [7], or timed process algebra [8], [9], providing alternative solutions to propose a general framework for describing all the relevant aspects without assuming a specific task model.

We are trying to propose an alternative method based on a different time abstraction, i.e., logical time. We think logical time and multiform time bases offer some flexibility to unify functional requirements and performance constraints. We rely on the Clock Constraint Specification Language (CCSL) [10] to give a concrete syntax to handle logical time, logical clocks and logical clock constraints. We claim that after encoding the scheduling problem in CCSL, finding a schedule for a CCSL model gives also a schedule for the encoded task model. Now, even though CCSL has been there for a while, there is no decidability result on finding a valid schedule. That is, it is still open to determine the existence of a valid schedule for a given set of CCSL constraints. Our ultimate goal is to find a schedule for the task model, which can be generic and tailored to particular situations and we do not assume a generic task model in our approach.

We also look for practical and efficient algorithms to find a schedule for CCSL. Finite-state automata is not expressive enough to encode all CCSL constraints [11]. It may cause state-explosion problem in the transformation [12], [13]. We focus on SMT-based solutions, considering the good practical results of SMT-based techniques and insufficiency of SAT ( [11]). After introducing CCSL and the scheduling problem of CCSL we describe a simple task model in CCSL and discuss how different our solution is from classical approaches.

div.head: II. THE CLOCK CONSTRAINT SPECIFICATION LANGUAGE
div.p: In CCSL, clocks are first-class citizens used to describe relationships between events in a system. Clocks record logical order of event occurrences instead of physical dates. No global physical time is presumed for the clocks. This loose composition of clocks define a polychronous specification of the expected causal and temporal behavior of a system. A clock ticks according to the occurrence of its associated event. Besides, a clock can memorize the number of ticks it has made. A schedule defines a partial order between the ticks of the clocks and captures what happens during one particular execution. For instance, a clock may represent the sequence of dispatch instants of a task, its preemption points, or its normal termination instants. No assumption is made on the periodicity of the task only that it is meant to execute several times (possibly infinitely many times). A clock may also represent the communications between tasks or the acquisition of a shared resource by a task.

div.head: Definition 1 (Logical clock).
div.p: A logical clock c is an infinite sequence of ticks (c i ) i∈N + with each c i being tick or idle, where N + denotes the set of all the non-zero natural numbers.

The value of c i denotes whether an event associated with c occurs or not at step i. If c i is tick, then the event occurs, otherwise not. In particular, we use 1 (resp. 0) to denote a special clock that always (resp. never) ticks at each step.
div.formula: Definition 2 (Schedule). Given a set C of clocks, a schedule of C is a total function δ : N + → 2 C such that ∀i ∈ N + , δ(i) = {c ∈ C | c i = tick} and δ(i) = ∅.
div.p: δ(i) is the subset of C such that c ∈ δ(i) if and only it ticks at step i. The condition δ(i) = ∅ says that it is not allowed that no clocks tick at a step. Such a step is called empty, which is trivial in that one can add or remove finite amount of empty steps without any impact on the schedulability of the constraints. We exclude them from schedules for succinctness.

As a clock can memorize the number of ticks that it has made, we use history to represent the memorization. Definition 3 (History). Given a schedule δ : N + → 2 C on a set C of clocks, a history of δ is a function χ δ : C × N + → N such that for each clock c ∈ C and natural number i ∈ N + :

χ δ (c, i) represents the number of the ticks that clock c has made immediately before step i. Note that the tick of c at step i is not counted in χ δ (c, i). For simplicity, we also write χ for χ δ if it is clear from the context.

There are eleven kinds of constraints in CCSL. Four of them are binary relations, used to define the precedence, causality, subclocking, and exclusion relations. Other seven are used to define new clocks using existing ones.

Precedence of events in real-time systems is very common. A clock c 1 precedes c 2 , denoted by c 1 ≺ c 2 , if c 1 must occur earlier than c 2 . Suppose that there is an unbounded buffer with two operations fetch and store, which respectively fetch data from and store data into the buffer. Fetch is only allowed when the buffer is nonempty. If the buffer is initially empty, store operation must strictly precede fetch operation. We usually say that store precedes fetch, which is represented by the following CCSL constraint.

div.head: store ≺ fetch
div.p: The same construct can be used to represent reentrant tasks and replacing store by start and fetch by finish. The size of the buffer indicates the degree of reentrance. It can also represent a mutex or many other FIFO-based behaviors.

The constraint can be more generic to specify more general scenarios, i.e., to give a specific number of occurrence differences of two operations before the precedence takes effect. For instance, if the buffer is not initially empty, fetch operations can be performed prior to any store operations.

div.p: A causality relation, denoted by c 1 c 2 , specifies that the occurrence of c 2 must be caused by the occurrence of c 1 . It is equivalent to say that at any moment c 1 must have ticked at least as many times as c 2 has. The subclock and exclusion constraints can be also defined likewise. We say c 1 is a subclock of c 2 , denoted by c 1 ⊆ c 2 , if c 1 occurs at some step, then c 2 must occur at this step as well. Two clocks c 1 and c 2 are exclusive, denoted by c 1 # c 2 , if they cannot occur simultaneously at the same step.

Other constraints (called expressions) are used to define new clocks based on existing ones. Union and intersection are the two simplest constraints, which define the union and intersection of two clocks, respectively. Let u be a union of two clocks c 1 and c 2 , u ticks if and only if c 1 or c 2 ticks. Similarly, let i be the intersection of c 1 and c 2 . Then, i ticks if and only if both c 1 and c 2 tick.

Another two kinds of constraints are called infimum and supremum. By infimum, one can define a new clock inf from two clocks c 1 and c 2 , such that inf is the slowest clock among those that are faster than c 1 and c 2 . In other words, a clock inf is an infimum of two clocks c 1 and c 2 if and only if inf is the slowest clock that has ticked at least as many times as both c 1 and c 2 .
Likewise, a supremum can be defined, such that sup is the fastest clock among those that are slower than c 1 and c 2 .

These two constructs are useful when trying to express delay requirements between two events of the system. Minimizing (or bounding) the distance between infimum and supremum is a way to ensure that two events are never too far apart.

These notions extends the equivalent behavior usually defined relative to physical time. div.head: III. SCHEDULING PROBLEM
div.p: Given a CCSL constraint φ and a schedule δ, we use δ |= φ to denote that δ satisfies φ. Given a set Φ of CCSL constraints, a schedule δ satisfies Φ, denoted by δ |= Φ, if and only if δ |= φ for all constraints φ ∈ Φ.
A fundamental question for CCSL to answer is whether there exists a schedule satisfying a given set of constraints.
Definition 5 (Scheduling problem). Given a set Φ of CCSL constraints, the scheduling problem of CCSL is to determine whether there exists a schedule δ such that δ |= Φ.

Solving the scheduling problem for CCSL is challenging for the two main reasons. First, schedules are essentially infinite, i.e., defined on all the natural numbers. Second, some constraints such as precedence and delayFor are stateful, i.e., constraints depend on their history behaviors. As a first step to tackle this challenging problem, we propose to encode CCSL constraints into an SMT solver and to reduce the scheduling problem to the bounded case and the periodic cases that were introduced in the earlier works [14], [15].

We can distinguish three different case for a CCSL specification. The first case is when in all the valid schedules all the clocks can execute infinitely often. In other words, there is no conflicts and the scheduling problem is merely a problem of constructing the solutions in a constructive and operational way. The second cases is when after some time some clocks cannot tick anymore. This situation is akin to a partial deadlock. The scheduling problem consists mainly in finding the path finite path that inevitably leads to this partial deadlock. The final case is when some paths lead to infinite valid behaviors while other lead to partial deadlocks. In that case, the scheduling problem is to avoid the so-called "bad" paths" to remain on the valid ones.

In the first case, different solutions depart from each other in a non-essential way, they are schedule-insensitive. It is mainly a reordering of the actions. From a pure schedulability point of view all the solutions are equivalent. However from a resource point of view, they might not be completely equivalent. Take for example, the example of store ≺ fetch. Having one hundred stores followed by one hundred fetch is valid possible schedule. Another valid schedule simply consists in alternating stores and fetches actions. In the first case, one needs a buffer of size one hundred to count all the stores before fetching. In the other case, one only needs a buffer of size one. For schedule-insensitive specifications, the problem become one of optimizing some arbitrary non-functional property by selecting the most suitable valid solution among all the possible ones.

div.head: IV. SIMPLE TASK MODEL
div.p: The point here is to show that we can reduce a standard real-time scheduling problem to finding a valid schedule for a CCSL specification. To make this point we show how we can incrementally build a task model that becomes more and more complex by adding CCSL constraints.

Let us consider a task t. One can model such a task by considering two logical clocks t s and t f that capture the start and finish of the task. Then the constraint t s ≺ t f captures the simple execution of a task with a duration. Note that this task can be re-rentrant. To forbid the re-entrance, one needs instead to write t s [1] ≺ t f . To specify a duration or a variable duration during a given interval, then one can simply write t f ≺ t s $ d on ms, where d is an integer and s is a clock that denotes a physical clock ticking every millisecond. This constraint can denote a maximum duration or a deadline. To make it a fix duration, one just has to replace the precedence by a coincidence. If the task is periodic then one can do the same to fix the starting date of the task the way there the finishing date is fixed or bounded.

Let us consider three tasks now t1, t2 and t3. Capturing a data dependency dependency between t1 and t2 can be done also using a precedence t1 f ≺ t2 s . Now if one wants to capture allocation constraints then we need to introduce new clocks acq and rel that model the acquisition or release of a resource, i.e., say a processor or a core. acq = t1 s + t3 s , rel = t1 f + t3 f , acq [1] ≺ rel is a way to allocate task t1 and t3 to the same resource. Adding t1 s # t3 s makes this access exclusive and would forbid the two tasks to execute simultaneously.

Finally note that dealing with preemption would require additional constraints but the idea behind CCSL is to add constraints in a cumulative way reducing step by step the set of possible valid schedules. When no schedule are possible, there are too many constraints and thus the task model is not schedulable. Then there is only one solution, then the task model is schedule. When there are many solutions we need to explore the different solutions to decide whether there are schedule-insensitive or not, and whether some bad paths can be reached or whether there are all equivalent with regards to non-functional properties. First encouraging results [16] show that we can encode CCSL specifications into SMT problems and use SMT solvers to find whether there are valid schedules. Bad paths and schedule-insensitiveness can also be checked in favorable conditions [11], however, there is no general decision procedure in the general case. The experience shows that in most real-time schedulability cases, we return to computing the hyper-period for a solution, we thus restrict to the favorable case where checking for a periodic schedule becomes possible and efficient using SMT [16].

div.head: V. RELATED WORK AND DISCUSSION
div.p: Besides CCSL, many specific scheduling frameworks have indeed been introduced to provide schedulability analysis and efficient scheduling generation. We are not trying to compete with these approaches, but we aim to provide an alternate method in CCSL. Two decision problems on CCSL, finding bad paths and schedule-insensitiveness, provide a general description of scheduling approaches, without loss of generality.

Most of the frameworks, e.g., timed automata [3], [4], [5], timed petri nets [6], [7], timed process algebra [8], [9], rely on "physical-by-nature" timings. The distinctive difference is that their systems are presented as synchronously timed on a single global continuous time, with various timed events being constrained by value relations between real-valued clocks. Those physical clocks are devices measuring physical time as it elapses and very different from our logical clocks. Thus, correspondence should rather be between our logical clocks and the timed events. Data flow graphs provide scheduling models where the initial constraints are less on timing and more on dependencies or on exclusive resource allocation. The resulting schedules are almost always of modulo periodic nature, matching the CCSL expressiveness. A possible schedule we provide, a sequence of steps filled with simultaneous clock ticks at each step, often falls into periodic nature too [17] (state space of a CCSL specification may be finite while a schedule is usually infinite [11]). When periodic, the schedule can be efficiently encoded as a table. Some previous works [10], [18] focus on the relations between data flow graphs and CCSL.

We take full advantages of CCSL in modeling, such as the flexibility provided by logical time, multi-form time bases, unified expressing of both functional requirements and extra performance constraints. More detailed example based discussions of these advantages could be found in papers [19], [20]. In this paper, we also study how a general translation expanding the semantics of CCSL into an adequate model could provide a generic way to figure out whether a specification does admit at least one solution (schedulability) and then to produce one admissible schedule that may not be the optimal one, even when there is one. Some time, the optimality may be reached by adding further constraints that make explicit the optimality criterion.

Schedule-insensitiveness is akin to the notion of the confluence in synchronous process algebra [21]. It also seems closely related to the conflict-freeness in Process Networks [22], [23] and the weak endochrony in SIGNAL [24]. It boils down to the desynchronization of synchronous models into asynchronous implementations, only requiring that interleaving of actions does not depend on the order in which the actions are executed, i.e., what happens along the different paths is not relevant. While our work concentrates on the insensitiveness of time placement of different schedules, the history of each clock is crucial. The mix of synchrony and asynchrony and the clock terminations in CCSL also rise the complexity of our checking. In the future, we want to inspect how relations between clocks can be used to detect unschedulability and scheduleinsensitiveness at construction time prior to building (explicitly or not) the full state space. The topology of constraint relations may give some precious indications on what is schedulable or not, just like hierarchy trees in synchronous languages are used for similar purposes.
